title: How Big Was the Biggest Animal Ever?

lines: This is a blue whale, the biggest animal alive today.
The largest ones can grow to about thirty-three metres. That is one hundred ten feet.
Imagine you are swimming right next to one.
You would need about nineteen people, lying head to toe, to match its length.
It is longer than two city buses parked end to end,
and longer than a basketball court.
But is it the biggest animal that has ever lived?
Three giants from the past have challenged it.
A monster shark. Dinosaurs that may have been even longer.
And a fossil whale from Peru that scientists once thought was even heavier.
Today we measure every one of them, side by side,
next to a person and a bus, to find the true champion.
Chapter one. The blue whale.
Blue whales live in every ocean on Earth.
They are mammals, like us. They breathe air, and they feed their babies milk.
Let's measure. On our grid, each line is one metre.
Here is a person, one point seven five metres tall. And a city bus, twelve metres long.
And here is the blue whale.
The very largest, in the cold seas around Antarctica, reach about thirty-three metres. Most are a bit smaller.
Blue whales may live for eighty to ninety years.
And they are not monsters. They eat almost nothing but tiny animals.
But length is only half the story.
To know who is truly biggest, we also have to weigh them.
We measure weight in tonnes. One tonne is one thousand kilograms.
An adult male African elephant weighs about six tonnes.
The largest blue whales can weigh about one hundred fifty tonnes.
That is roughly as heavy as twenty-five adult male African elephants.
How does an animal get that heavy?
By eating some of the smallest animals in the sea: krill.
Krill are small, shrimp-like animals, up to about six centimetres long.
Alone they are tiny. But they gather in huge swarms, and that is a feast.
A blue whale takes a giant gulp of water full of krill.
Then it pushes the water out through bristly plates called baleen, and swallows the food.
The biggest blue whales may eat up to six tons of krill in a single day,
about the weight of a large elephant, every day.
So far: the blue whale can reach thirty-three metres and one hundred fifty tonnes.
But twenty million years ago, something with much bigger teeth ruled the sea.
Chapter two. Megalodon.
Megalodon was a giant shark.
It lived from about twenty-three million years ago until about three point six million years ago.
To feel how long ago that is:
people like us have existed for only about three hundred thousand years. Megalodon vanished more than ten times earlier.
We know megalodon mostly from its teeth.
A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the bendy material in your ears and nose, and it rarely becomes a fossil.
The largest megalodon teeth are about eighteen centimetres long, roughly the length of a hand.
This jaw is a modern model, sized from teeth like these.
Megalodon was a hunter.
One study suggests an adult could eat prey as large as a killer whale.
Now, the size. Here is a great white shark, the biggest hunting shark alive today.
It reaches about six metres.
Megalodon estimates range from about sixteen metres to as much as twenty-four.
Scientists still argue, because only teeth and a few backbones survive.
The best clue is a row of megalodon backbones found in Belgium, about eleven metres long.
But the head and the tail are missing, so scientists must estimate them.
Some scientists think megalodon was chunky, like a great white.
Others think it was slimmer and longer, more like a lemon shark.
Even at its largest estimate, megalodon was shorter than the biggest blue whales.
And it was lighter. A sixteen-metre megalodon may have weighed about sixty tonnes.
Even a twenty-four-metre one was probably under one hundred.
So far: megalodon was a true giant, but shorter and lighter than the biggest blue whales.
On land, though, some animals grew even longer.
Chapter three. Titans on land.
These are sauropods: plant-eating dinosaurs with long necks and long tails, walking on four legs.
This one is Apatosaurus.
Apatosaurus was about twenty-two metres long, nearly two buses.
And it was not even one of the biggest.
The true giants came later, in what is now Argentina,
about one hundred million years ago, in the Cretaceous period.
The Cretaceous was the last period of the dinosaurs.
It ended sixty-six million years ago, when a huge asteroid hit the Earth.
Meet Argentinosaurus. This skeleton is a full-size cast, a copy.
It was rebuilt from just a handful of real bones: some backbones, ribs and a leg bone.
Because so few bones survive, its length is uncertain: about thirty to thirty-five metres.
That may match, or even beat, the blue whale.
Its relative Patagotitan was first estimated at thirty-seven metres.
Later studies shrank it to about thirty-one.
But on the scale, the dinosaurs lose.
Most estimates put them between about fifty and ninety-six tonnes, well below a big blue whale.
Why not heavier? On land, every kilogram must be carried by legs.
Sauropods had pillar-like legs and bones filled with air pockets. But gravity still sets a limit.
So far: the longest dinosaurs may have matched the blue whale for length, but weighed far less.
Then, in twenty twenty-three, a fossil whale claimed the crown.
Chapter four. The challengers.
In twenty twenty-three, scientists described Perucetus colossus,
an ancient whale that lived about thirty-nine million years ago, in what is now Peru.
Its bones were incredibly thick and heavy.
From them, the team estimated a weight of eighty-five to three hundred forty tonnes.
Only a few of its bones have been found: thirteen backbones, four ribs and part of a hip.
No skull. So its shape and size are partly a guess.
In the middle of that range, it would beat the largest blue whale.
Headlines called it a contender for the heaviest animal ever.
But a year later, two other scientists checked the math again.
Heavy bones, they argued, do not mean a heavy body. Their estimate: sixty to one hundred fourteen tonnes.
Huge, but lighter than the biggest blue whales.
The crown stayed where it was.
One more challenger. In England, a girl and her father found pieces of a giant jawbone on a beach.
It belonged to Ichthyotitan, a sea reptile from two hundred two million years ago.
Ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles shaped a bit like dolphins.
They breathed air, but they never came onto land.
From two jawbones, scientists estimate it was up to about twenty-five metres long.
With so few bones, nobody knows its weight. And it still falls short of the blue whale.
So far: no fossil challenger has beaten the blue whale on weight.
So why is the biggest animal ever alive right now, and not in the past?
Chapter five. Why now?
First, water. In the sea, water pushes up on a body and supports its weight.
So a whale does not need legs to carry one hundred fifty tonnes.
Second, food. About three million years ago, ocean currents changed.
Cold water rising from the deep fed huge, packed swarms of krill in some seasons.
Bigger whales could swim farther between these feasts, and take in more food with every gulp.
Over time, whales grew into giants.
Could whales grow even bigger one day?
Studies of feeding whales suggest the biggest are close to the limit of how much food they can gather.
So the giant whales are recent.
For most of their history, baleen whales were much smaller.
Which means something surprising.
You live at the same time as the biggest animal that has ever lived. Not in the past. Right now.
But in the last century, whalers hunted blue whales almost to extinction.
Today they are protected, and slowly coming back.
So far: water carries the whale's weight, and seasonal krill feasts feed it.
Now, let's put every giant side by side.
Chapter six. The final line-up.
Here they all are, to the same scale.
A person. A bus. A great white shark. Megalodon. Ichthyotitan. Perucetus.
And on land, Argentinosaurus.
Some may have been as long as the blue whale. As far as we know, none was as heavy.
On length, it is close. Argentinosaurus, maybe thirty-five metres. The blue whale, about thirty-three.
Patagotitan, about thirty-one. Ichthyotitan, up to twenty-five. Megalodon, up to twenty-four.
On the scale: the blue whale, up to about one hundred fifty tonnes.
Every challenger lands below it.
The biggest animal that has ever lived is alive today: the blue whale.
But fossils keep surprising us. One new bone could change this ranking.
So here is my question for you:
which of these giants would you most like to see alive, up close? Tell me in the comments.
